Measure the shot angle with the camera

Accuracy depends on the phone\'s sensors, typically within 0.5–1°. Calibrating (two aims at one point, the second with the phone turned over) removes the camera\'s tilt in the phone, not the sensor\'s own error.

The camera sits slightly tilted in the phone body, which shifts every reading by the same amount. Two aims at one point remove it:

1. Hold the phone as you will measure (portrait or landscape), ideally resting on something steady, and put the crosshair on a distant, sharp point.
2. Tap Calibrate: the first aim is kept and ✓ 1/2 shows.
3. Turn the phone over: portrait upside down, or landscape the other way round. Put the crosshair on the same point.
4. Tap again.

Portrait and landscape are calibrated separately and kept on this phone. The sensor's own error (typically 0.5–1°) stays.
For the second aim, turn the phone over: portrait upside down, or landscape the other way round.

Settings, Profiles: add your rifle with its scope and zero, and your load (from the library or your own data). The Rifle tab picks the rifle and load in use and whether the suppressor is on.

Conditions: set the wind, temperature, pressure and altitude, and the shot angle if you shoot up or down. The button under the altitude fills it from your location (terrain map or GPS, set in Settings) and also sets the latitude; you can still type both.

DOPE gives the scope settings for every range; Target gives the correction for one distance, drawn on your reticle.

Turn on Suppressor in the rifle section of the rifle profile. Then, in the zero section, say whether you zeroed with it on (Suppressed) or off (Bare), and enter where the impact goes in the other state, up and right from the zero in the turret unit (negative for down or left). Shoot a group in that state at your zero range to find it. Switching which state the zero was shot in flips the signs.\n\nOn the Rifle tab, switch the suppressor on or off. When it differs from the zero, every correction includes the shift and the rifle on the Rifle tab icon carries a suppressor while it is on.

Pick the unit marked on the turrets. MRAD: 0.1 MRAD is 1 cm at 100 m, so a "1 cm at 100 m" click is 0.1 MRAD. MOA: 1.047 in at 100 yd, 2.91 cm at 100 m. SMOA (shooter's MOA, also IPHY): 1 in at 100 yd, 2.78 cm at 100 m. Some scopes sold as MOA are SMOA; the manual says which. Mixing them up puts the DOPE 4.7 % off, about 40 cm at 1000 m.

The correction is what the turret really moves for what is marked on it. Few turrets track exactly, and 1–3 % off is common. Measure it with a tall-target test:
1. Hang a tall target with a plumb line or a level vertical line, at a distance you measured with a tape (100 m is enough).
2. Level the scope and shoot a group at the bottom of the target with the zero dialled.
3. Dial up a large correction, e.g. 10 MRAD or 30 MOA, keep the same aim point and shoot another group.
4. Measure the distance between the two group centres in cm and turn it into the turret unit: MRAD = cm ÷ (distance in m × 0.1), MOA = cm ÷ (distance in m × 0.0291), SMOA = cm ÷ (distance in m × 0.0278).
5. Correction = measured ÷ dialled.

Example: dialled 10 MRAD at 100 m, the groups are 98 cm apart. Measured 98 ÷ (100 × 0.1) = 9.8 MRAD, correction 9.8 ÷ 10 = 0.98. For a 10 MRAD correction the app then tells you to dial 10.2. Leave the field blank for a turret that tracks true.

An MOA turret that tests at about 0.955 is SMOA: pick SMOA and leave the correction blank. A result far from 1 more often means a wrong distance than a bad turret, so check that first.

The correction applies to both turrets. The DOPE table, the dialling advice and BC truing all use the corrections.

The zero range and the temperature and pressure on the day you zeroed. The app computes the bore angle that hits at that range in those conditions, and keeps it for every other shot.\n\nIf you zeroed in very different weather, entering it moves the whole DOPE by the difference.

QNH is the pressure reduced to sea level: weather reports, forecasts and airports give it. With QNH the app also needs the altitude, to work out the pressure where you stand.

Station pressure is what a barometer reads where you are: a Kestrel or a Garmin watch. It needs no altitude.

Pick the one you actually have; using QNH as station pressure at altitude is a large error.

The velocity you measured with this rifle and this load, if you entered one in the rifle\'s zero section. Otherwise the load\'s reference velocity, which was measured in its test barrel: a shorter barrel is usually slower.\n\nThe velocity follows the air temperature with the load\'s powder sensitivity.
How do I enter the wind?

The dial is a wind clock inside a compass ring. Tap it to unlock it (its rim turns coloured); a tap anywhere off its round face locks it again, so scrolling over it changes nothing.

Once unlocked, tap or drag inside the clock to set where the wind comes from. On the ring you set the azimuth: in the shooter view (line of fire up) drag the ring to turn it; with north up, tap or drag the ring where the target is.

The round button in the dial's corner switches between the two views; its red needle always points north. Under the dial you see how much of the wind blows across the line of fire and how much along it.

Forecast fills in the wind for your location and a chosen time window; the wind bracket on Target shows the lightest and strongest case.
How do I measure the shot angle?

Tap the camera between Shot angle and Cant and aim the crosshair at the target: the gravity sensor gives the angle.\n\nCalibrate once per orientation: aim at a mark, then turn the phone over and aim again. This removes the camera\'s tilt in the phone.
How do I read the Target screen?

Set the distance with the field, the arrows or the slider. The corners of the reticle say what to dial and what to hold for elevation and windage; the red points are where the bullet goes at each distance.\n\nWhether each axis is dialed or held is set per reticle in Settings. Dial corrections are whole clicks, holds are to 0.05.
How does the moving target work?

Tick Moving target, enter its speed and set its course on the small dial in the reticle\'s corner (tap it first to unlock it): up is away from you, right is to the right.\n\nThe blue point is where to hold so the bullet meets the target, using the time of flight.

For each range: drop, elevation and clicks, wind drift and windage, velocity, energy, time of flight and Mach. Its range and step are set below it; tap the open tab or the arrow to fold the details at the top.\n\nThe cm columns say where the bullet goes: drop below the line of sight, drift with the wind. The MRAD or MOA and clicks columns are the correction to dial, with the turret correction from the rifle profile: up has no mark, ↓ means dial down (short of the zero), and R or L is the windage.
Where does the altitude come from?

Settings, Data sources, Altitude from: the terrain map or GPS. The button under the altitude on Conditions reads it; the field can always be typed in. The same location fix also sets the latitude for Coriolis (untick Latitude from location to keep it). The terrain map gives the ground height at your location (a 1 m lidar model in Poland, a 90 m model elsewhere) and needs the internet. GPS works anywhere under open sky, also in stealth mode; the height is converted to above sea level.\n\nThe altitude matters only with QNH: with station pressure the app does not need it.
How do I use a Garmin watch?

Install the free Station Pressure app on the watch from the Connect IQ Store and in Settings, Data sources, set Pressure measurement to Garmin; the Test button there checks the connection. The Garmin button under the pressure on Conditions reads the watch\'s barometer as station pressure.
How does the wind forecast work?

Forecast under the wind dial gets the wind for your location from Open-Meteo. Pick the hours you will shoot on the chart and the shooting height, then Use fills in the wind, and the atmosphere too if you leave that on. The ? in the forecast window explains the chart.
How do I import chronograph data?

Chrono on the Rifle tab opens a chronograph file (Labradar, Labradar LX, Garmin Xero, Athlon Rangecraft, MagnetoSpeed or any table with a velocity column) or lets you type the velocities. You can also share a file from another app straight into this one.\n\nYou see the average, SD and ES; shots that look misread are flagged, and each shot can be ticked in or out. Save the velocity for this rifle only, or for the load (all rifles); it is corrected to the load\'s reference powder temperature.
What are the tools on the Target tab?

Under the reticle, each card is a tool for the chosen distance:

Wind bracket: the holds for the lightest and strongest wind you expect, drawn on a slice of your reticle, and the spread between them.

Range error: where the bullet lands if the distance is off by a few metres, and the window of distances that still hits a target of your size.

Temperature: how the velocity and elevation change if the powder is warmer or colder.

Hit probability: the chance of a first-round hit from your group size, velocity SD, and how well you know the wind and the distance.

Ranging with the reticle: the distance from the target's size and how many MRAD or MOA it reads.

BC from range data: the BC that matches a measured drop or downrange velocity, saved to the load or as a copy.
How do I read the charts?

The charts show how a correction changes with distance, wind or azimuth, with the current value marked. Drag a finger along a chart to read any point; the reading stays when you lift it. On the charts by distance, hold the finger still to make that the target distance. A tap clears the reading.\n\nEach chart can be turned off in Settings, Display, Charts; a chart that is off is not worked out either.
Sign in with Google in Settings to sync between phones. Export writes all profiles to a file you can import again, here or in the web version.
How do I update the app?
Settings, About, Check for update downloads the newest build and opens the installer. Turn on the check at start to be told when there is one.
How far can I trust it?

It is only as good as its inputs: muzzle velocity, BC, the zero and the wind matter most. Confirm the dope with live fire at the distances you use, and correct the velocity until the DOPE matches your hits.

The chart shows the next hours of the forecast: the dark bar is the mean wind, the light part the gusts, and the arrow above each hour where the wind blows (12 up is down range; in Settings you can switch the arrows to true bearings, north up).

Pick the time you will shoot: tap an hour, drag the shaded window, or drag its edges to make it longer or shorter. The arrows under the chart show later hours.

The forecast is for 10 m above the ground; near the ground the wind is slower. Shooting height scales it: ×1.0 for 10 m, ×0.8 for about 2 m in open ground, ×0.67 for about 2 m among trees or buildings.

The speed is the mean of the hourly values and the direction that of the mean wind vector. If the direction changes a lot in the window, a warning shows. A forecast is a starting point; read the wind on the range.

Airplane mode does not always turn off Wi-Fi and Bluetooth: Android remembers if you turned them back on in airplane mode. Check both, turn off Wi-Fi and Bluetooth scanning in the location settings, and NFC and UWB (ultra-wideband, for item trackers and car keys) where the phone has them.

Swipe down twice, tap the pencil and drag the Stealth tile into the panel.

The aircraft icon on the Rifle tab, Settings → Stealth mode or the Stealth quick settings tile turns it on. The app then makes no connections: no forecast, terrain height, sync, bullet database, store or update checks, and no Garmin watch unless you allow it in Settings. GPS stays on, from the satellites alone (it only receives); you can turn it off for stealth mode in Settings. Without network help and airplane mode the system may still download GPS assistance data, and the first fix can take a few minutes.\n\nAndroid lets no app turn off the phone\'s radios, so the stealth window lists them: red with waves means it still transmits; each button opens its settings. Airplane mode does not always turn off Wi-Fi and Bluetooth (Android remembers if you turned them back on), and Wi-Fi and Bluetooth scanning in the location settings keeps going without them. NFC and UWB (ultra-wideband, for item trackers and car keys) transmit at short range. The Garmin watch keeps calling for the phone until you also turn off its phone connection. The bar at the top can be hidden in Settings.
